title: Phase 2: Replace tokio sync primitives with asupersync
description:
# Phase 2: Replace tokio sync primitives

## Goal
Replace all tokio::sync primitives (Mutex, RwLock, Semaphore) with asupersync equivalents across the codebase.

## Scope
- tokio::sync::Mutex → asupersync::sync::Mutex (with guard obligation tracking)
- tokio::sync::RwLock → asupersync::sync::RwLock (with guard obligation tracking)
- tokio::sync::Semaphore/OwnedSemaphorePermit → asupersync::sync::Semaphore (with permit obligation)

## Key difference: Obligation tracking
asupersync sync primitives enforce that guards/permits are properly released. The obligation system uses LeakChecker and ObligationVar to catch forgotten guards at scope exit.

## Affected files (primary)
- crates/wa-core/src/pool.rs — Semaphore + Mutex for connection pooling (CRITICAL)
- crates/wa-core/src/runtime.rs — RwLock for shared state
- crates/wa-core/src/mcp.rs — Mutex for tool registration
- crates/wa-core/src/web.rs — Mutex/RwLock for request handling
- Multiple other modules using Arc<Mutex<T>> and Arc<RwLock<T>>

## Migration pattern
```rust
// Before (tokio)
use tokio::sync::Mutex;
let data = Arc::new(Mutex::new(value));
let guard = data.lock().await;

// After (asupersync)
use asupersync::sync::Mutex;
let data = Arc::new(Mutex::new(value));
let guard = data.lock(cx).await?;  // Note: takes cx, returns Outcome
```

## Acceptance criteria
- All tokio::sync::{Mutex, RwLock, Semaphore} replaced
- Guard obligations properly tracked
- Existing tests pass with new primitives
- No deadlock regressions

## Concurrency verification
- **Loom model checking**: Use Loom to model-check ALL replaced sync primitives. Specifically:
  - Mutex: verify mutual exclusion, no deadlocks under all thread interleavings
  - RwLock: verify readers-writer invariant (multiple readers OR single writer), no starvation
  - Semaphore: verify permit count invariant never goes negative, FIFO fairness under contention
  - Add `tests/loom_sync.rs` with `#[test]` functions wrapped in `loom::model(|| { ... })` for each primitive.

## Benchmark requirements
- **Criterion benchmarks**: Compare tokio vs asupersync performance for each replaced primitive. Add `benches/sync_primitives.rs` measuring:
  - Uncontended lock/unlock latency (Mutex, RwLock)
  - Contended lock/unlock with N=2,4,8 tasks
  - Semaphore acquire/release throughput
  - Guard obligation tracking overhead (should be negligible in release builds)
  - Include both `tokio` and `asupersync` benchmark groups for direct A/B comparison.
close_reason: Implemented sync verification artifacts; rch-compiled loom_sync and sync_primitives successfully, with loom execution attempt blocked by rch queue_timeout/fail-open infra

title: [EPIC] FrankenTerm Scripting Engine — Lua + WASM Dual Runtime
description:
# FrankenTerm Scripting Engine — Lua + WASM Dual Runtime

## Strategic Decision (2026-02-10)
After debate, we chose Option C: keep Lua AND add WASM via wasmtime. This gives us:
- **Backward compatibility** with existing WezTerm Lua configs (huge ecosystem)
- **Modern extensibility** via WASM (any language → .wasm → runs sandboxed)
- **Migration path**: Lua = legacy/quick scripting, WASM = serious extensions, over time WASM primary

## Why NOT the other options
- **Option A (Lua only)**: Keeps C build dep (mlua+LuaJIT), single language, no sandbox
- **Option B (WASM only)**: Breaks every existing WezTerm config, too disruptive
- **Option D (V8)**: +30MB binary, C++ dep, overkill for terminal emulator

## Architecture: ScriptingEngine trait
Both engines implement a common `ScriptingEngine` trait:
```rust
pub trait ScriptingEngine: Send + Sync {
    fn eval_config(&self, path: &Path) -> Result<TerminalConfig>;
    fn register_hook(&self, event: &str, handler: ExtensionHandler) -> Result<HookId>;
    fn fire_event(&self, event: &str, payload: &dyn ToDynamic) -> Result<Vec<Action>>;
    fn load_extension(&self, manifest: &ExtensionManifest) -> Result<ExtensionId>;
}
```

## Feature flags
- `lua` (default) — enables mlua/LuaJIT, wezterm.lua config compat
- `wasm` — enables wasmtime, WASM extension loading
- `scripting-all` — both lua + wasm (for development/testing)
- `no-lua` — compiles out all Lua paths (headless/minimal builds)

## WASM runtime choice: wasmtime
- **Rust-native** (Bytecode Alliance, same org as wasm-tools)
- ~5MB binary overhead (vs ~30MB for V8)
- Full WASI support (filesystem, env vars, stdio)
- Component Model support (structured types, not just i32)
- Used by Zellij for plugins — proven in terminal space

## Build time impact
- Lua only: ~36s clean (LuaJIT C compilation is single-threaded)
- WASM only: ~20s clean (wasmtime is pure Rust, parallelizes well)
- Both: ~40s clean (but most users only enable one)
- no-lua: ~15s clean (minimal build)

## Extension package format (.ftx)
FrankenTerm eXtension bundles: ZIP containing manifest.toml + *.wasm + assets.
Can also contain Lua scripts for backward compat.

## Phases
1. Make Lua optional (feature flags in config, mux, luahelper)
2. Define ScriptingEngine trait abstraction
3. Add wasmtime + WASI integration
4. Implement WasmEngine
5. Build extension system
6. Config format evolution (TOML + WASM evaluation)
7. Migration tooling + documentation

## Relationship to other work
- Depends on wa-2umk2 (in-tree source ownership — can modify config/mux crates)
- FrankenMux (wa-2dd4s) benefits from WASM plugin panes (like Zellij)
- Ghostty analysis (wa-3bja) may reveal additional extension points
- asupersync (wa-e34d9) provides the async runtime for WASM I/O

title: Define ScriptingEngine trait abstraction and multi-engine dispatcher
Extension lifecycle management (install, update, remove)
description:
# Extension Lifecycle Management (Install, Update, Remove)

## Why
Extensions need a well-defined lifecycle: discovery → installation → loading → updating → removal. This bead covers the management commands and infrastructure.

## Lifecycle states
```
           ┌──────────┐
           │ available │ (in registry or local .ftx)
           └────┬─────┘
                │ install
           ┌────▼─────┐
           │ installed │ (on disk, not loaded)
           └────┬─────┘
                │ enable (on startup or manual)
           ┌────▼─────┐
           │  loaded   │ (WASM compiled, hooks registered)
           └────┬─────┘
                │ disable / error
           ┌────▼─────┐
           │ disabled  │ (installed but not loaded)
           └──────────┘
```

## CLI commands
```bash
# Install from local .ftx file
frankenterm ext install path/to/extension.ftx

# List installed extensions
frankenterm ext list
# Output:
# NAME         VERSION  ENGINE  STATUS   HOOKS
# my-theme     1.0.0    wasm    loaded   config.reload, pane.focus
# lua-compat   0.2.0    lua     loaded   *
# broken-ext   1.0.0    wasm    error    (load failed: missing export)

# Show extension details
frankenterm ext show my-theme

# Disable (keep installed, don't load)
frankenterm ext disable my-theme

# Enable (load on next startup)
frankenterm ext enable my-theme

# Remove (delete from disk)
frankenterm ext remove my-theme

# Update from new .ftx
frankenterm ext update my-theme path/to/my-theme-2.0.0.ftx
```

## Extension directory structure
```
~/.local/share/frankenterm/extensions/
├── my-theme/
│   ├── extension.toml
│   ├── main.wasm
│   ├── assets/
│   └── .state.toml          # Managed by FrankenTerm (enabled/disabled, load errors)
├── lua-compat/
│   ├── extension.toml
│   └── main.lua
└── .registry.toml            # Index of all installed extensions
```

## macOS fallbacks
On macOS, extension directories also check:
- `~/Library/Application Support/FrankenTerm/extensions/`
Prefer XDG paths when XDG_DATA_HOME is set; fall back to macOS-native Application Support otherwise.

## Extension config in frankenterm.toml
```toml
[extensions]
search_paths = ["~/.local/share/frankenterm/extensions"]
auto_load = true  # Load all enabled extensions on startup

[extensions.my-theme]
enabled = true
config = { variant = "dark" }  # Extension-specific config

[extensions.lua-compat]
enabled = true
```

## Error handling
- Extension that fails to load → status=error, clear error message, don't block startup
- Extension that panics during event → catch, log, disable extension, continue
- Extension that exceeds fuel → terminate call, log warning, keep extension loaded
- Extension with wrong permissions → deny specific operations, don't disable

## Files
- frankenterm/scripting/src/lifecycle.rs (NEW — install/enable/disable/remove)
- frankenterm/scripting/src/registry.rs (NEW — extension index management)
- crates/wa/src/ext_commands.rs (NEW — CLI commands for ext management)

## Testing
- Test full lifecycle: install → enable → load → disable → remove
- Test extension with load error doesn't block startup
- Test extension update preserves config
- Test CLI commands output correct information
- Test extension.toml config override per extension
- **proptest**: Property-based tests for lifecycle state machine transitions — generate random sequences of lifecycle operations (install, enable, disable, remove, update) and verify that the state machine always ends in a valid state, that illegal transitions (e.g., enable an uninstalled extension, remove a loaded extension without disabling first) produce clear errors rather than corrupted state, and that the registry.toml index remains consistent after any sequence
- **criterion benchmarks**: Measure install/update latency — benchmark the full install pipeline (.ftx extraction, manifest validation, WASM compilation, registry update) for small and large packages, and benchmark update operations (diff detection, hot-reload vs cold-reload) to ensure install completes in <2s for typical extensions and update in <500ms

title: Dual-engine test suite (Lua + WASM equivalence, stress, compat)
description:
# Dual-Engine Test Suite (Lua + WASM)

## Why
Both scripting engines must be tested independently AND together. We need:
1. Unit tests for each engine implementation
2. Integration tests that verify both engines produce identical results
3. Stress tests for resource limits
4. Regression tests for backward compatibility

## Test structure

### Unit tests (per engine)
```
frankenterm/scripting/tests/
├── lua_engine_test.rs        # LuaEngine-specific tests
├── wasm_engine_test.rs       # WasmEngine-specific tests
├── dispatcher_test.rs        # Multi-engine dispatcher tests
├── sandbox_test.rs           # Security/sandbox tests
├── extension_test.rs         # Extension loading tests
└── fixtures/
    ├── configs/
    │   ├── basic.lua         # Lua config fixture
    │   ├── basic.toml        # TOML config fixture
    │   ├── basic.wasm        # WASM config fixture (compiled from Rust)
    │   ├── complex.lua       # Lua with conditionals/functions
    │   └── complex.wasm      # WASM equivalent of complex.lua
    ├── extensions/
    │   ├── hello.ftx         # Minimal extension
    │   ├── theme.ftx         # Theme-only extension
    │   ├── hooks.ftx         # Extension with event hooks
    │   ├── malicious.ftx     # Extension that tries to escape sandbox
    │   └── oom.ftx           # Extension that allocates too much memory
    └── wasm_modules/
        ├── hello.wasm        # Simple test module
        ├── infinite_loop.wasm # Fuel exhaustion test
        ├── oom.wasm          # Memory limit test
        └── config_eval.wasm  # Config evaluation module
```

### Equivalence tests (critical!)
Both engines should produce identical config for equivalent inputs:
```rust
#[test]
fn lua_and_toml_produce_same_config() {
    let lua_config = lua_engine.eval_config("fixtures/configs/basic.lua")?;
    let toml_config = toml_loader.load("fixtures/configs/basic.toml")?;
    assert_eq!(lua_config.font_size, toml_config.font_size);
    assert_eq!(lua_config.color_scheme, toml_config.color_scheme);
    // ... all fields
}
```

### Stress tests
- 100 extensions loaded simultaneously
- Extension that fires 10,000 events/second
- Extension with 1MB of compiled WASM
- 50 concurrent event handlers

### Backward compatibility tests
- Load every WezTerm example config from the WezTerm docs
- Verify they parse without error (when lua feature enabled)
- Verify key config values are correctly extracted

## Building WASM test fixtures
Test WASM modules are compiled from Rust source in a build.rs:
```rust
// frankenterm/scripting/tests/wasm_src/hello.rs
#[no_mangle]
pub extern "C" fn configure() -> i32 {
    // Return pointer to config JSON
    ...
}
```
Compiled with: `cargo build --target wasm32-wasip1 -p test-wasm-fixtures`

## CI integration
```yaml
# In GitHub Actions
- name: Test scripting (Lua only)
  run: cargo test -p scripting --features lua
  
- name: Test scripting (WASM only)
  run: cargo test -p scripting --features wasm

- name: Test scripting (both)
  run: cargo test -p scripting --features scripting-all

- name: Test scripting (neither — must compile!)
  run: cargo check -p scripting --no-default-features
```

## Files
- frankenterm/scripting/tests/ (NEW — test directory)
- frankenterm/scripting/tests/fixtures/ (NEW — test fixtures)
- frankenterm/scripting/tests/wasm_src/ (NEW — Rust sources for test WASM modules)
- frankenterm/scripting/build.rs (NEW — compile WASM test fixtures)

## Testing (meta)
- All tests pass with `--features lua`
- All tests pass with `--features wasm`
- All tests pass with `--features scripting-all`
- `cargo check --no-default-features -p scripting` compiles
- CI runs all four configurations

title: Extension author documentation, examples, and SDK
description:
# Extension Author Documentation and Examples

## Why
For the extension ecosystem to thrive, authors need clear documentation, examples, and an SDK. This bead covers creating the documentation and starter templates.

## Documentation structure
```
docs/extensions/
├── getting-started.md        # Quick start: create your first extension
├── architecture.md           # How the scripting engine works
├── api-reference.md          # Complete host function reference
├── permissions.md            # Permission model explained
├── lua-extensions.md         # Writing Lua extensions
├── wasm-extensions.md        # Writing WASM extensions (Rust, Go, etc.)
├── migration-guide.md        # wezterm.lua → frankenterm extension
├── examples/
│   ├── theme/                # Theme-only extension (no code)
│   ├── status-bar/           # Status bar extension (WASM)
│   ├── auto-dark-mode/       # OS dark mode detection (WASM)
│   ├── session-logger/       # Log session events (Lua)
│   └── keybinding-helper/    # Custom keybinding actions (WASM)
└── sdk/
    ├── rust-quickstart.md    # Rust SDK quick start
    └── debugging.md          # How to debug extensions
```

## Example: Theme extension (no code)
```
my-theme.ftx:
├── extension.toml
│   [extension]
│   name = "dracula-plus"
│   type = "theme"
│   [hooks]
│   on_config_reload = "apply_theme"
└── assets/
    └── colors.toml
        [colors]
        foreground = "#f8f8f2"
        background = "#282a36"
        cursor_bg = "#f8f8f2"
        ...
```

## Example: WASM extension (Rust SDK)
```rust
use frankenterm_extension_sdk::prelude::*;

#[ft_extension]
struct AutoDarkMode;

#[ft_hook("config.reload")]
fn apply_theme(event: ConfigReloadEvent) -> Result<Vec<Action>> {
    let is_dark = ft::env::get("COLORFGBG")
        .map(|v| v.starts_with("15;"))
        .unwrap_or(true);
    
    let scheme = if is_dark { "Dracula" } else { "Solarized Light" };
    Ok(vec![Action::SetConfig("color_scheme".into(), scheme.into())])
}
```

## frankenterm-extension-sdk crate
Publish as a separate crate on crates.io:
- Proc macros: `#[ft_extension]`, `#[ft_hook("event")]`
- Type-safe wrappers for all host functions
- Serde integration for payload serialization
- `cargo generate` template for new extensions

## Performance expectations for documentation
Documentation should include criterion benchmark expectations so extension authors can write performant extensions:
- Hook handler execution budget: <1ms per event handler call
- Extension load time budget: <500ms cold, <10ms cached
- Memory budget: 64MB per extension (configurable)
- Authors should include criterion benchmarks in their extension test suites to verify they meet these budgets

## Testing
- All example extensions compile and load successfully
- Documentation builds without broken links
- SDK crate compiles to wasm32-wasip1 target
- cargo generate template produces working extension

## Cross-references
- **wa-3dfxb.8** (package format): Documentation must cover the .ftx package structure, manifest fields, and packaging workflow in detail — the getting-started guide walks authors through creating their first .ftx package
- **wa-3dfxb.9** (extension API): The api-reference.md is the primary documentation for all host functions, event types, and SDK wrappers defined in wa-3dfxb.9 — keep the docs and API in sync

title: Native event hooks replacing Lua callbacks in hot paths
description:
# Native Event Hooks — Replace Lua Callbacks in Performance-Critical Paths

## Why
WezTerm fires Lua callbacks for events like update-status, user-var-changed, and pane output. These Lua calls are the #1 performance bottleneck (see bd-2oby). Under the dual-runtime strategy, we replace hot-path Lua callbacks with native Rust event hooks, while keeping Lua available for user-facing event handlers.

## Hot paths that must be native
| Event | Current | Frequency | Impact |
|-------|---------|-----------|--------|
| update-status | Lua callback | Every render (~60Hz) | Major |
| user-var-changed | Lua callback | Per pane output | Major |
| pane-output | Lua callback | Continuous | Critical |
| window-resized | Lua callback | On resize | Minor |

## What to build
1. Native Rust event bus (pub/sub) for hot-path events
2. Typed event payloads (no Lua value conversion overhead)
3. Priority-based dispatch (native handlers run first, then scripting engine)
4. Zero-allocation steady-state (pre-allocated event buffers)

### Event bus design
```rust
pub struct EventBus {
    native_handlers: HashMap<EventType, Vec<NativeHandler>>,
    script_handlers: Vec<HookRegistration>,  // From ScriptingEngine
}

pub type NativeHandler = Box<dyn Fn(&Event) -> Vec<Action> + Send + Sync>;
```

## Dispatch order
1. Native handlers (Rust code, zero overhead)
2. WASM extension handlers (sandboxed, ~100μs overhead)
3. Lua extension handlers (GIL, ~1ms overhead)

Native handlers handle the hot path. Scripting engine handlers are for user customization.

## Performance target
- Native event dispatch: <1μs per event
- WASM event dispatch: <100μs per event  
- Lua event dispatch: <1ms per event (existing baseline)
- Zero allocations in native handler path

## Files
- frankenterm/mux/src/events.rs (NEW — event bus)
- frankenterm/mux/src/tab.rs (replace Lua callbacks with event bus)
- frankenterm/config/src/hooks.rs (native config change hooks)

## Testing
- Benchmark: native vs Lua callback for update-status event
- Verify event ordering: native → WASM → Lua
- Verify all existing Lua events still fire (backward compat)
- Stress test: 10,000 events/second sustained
- **criterion benchmarks**: Measure native hook dispatch vs Lua callback overhead — benchmark the full dispatch path for update-status at 60Hz, comparing native Rust handlers, WASM handlers, and Lua handlers side-by-side; native dispatch must be >10x faster than Lua callback (target: <1μs native vs ~10-50μs Lua); also benchmark zero-allocation steady-state by verifying no heap allocations during sustained 10K events/second dispatch via `#[global_allocator]` counting
- **Loom model checking**: Use loom to verify concurrent hook dispatch correctness — model the EventBus with multiple producer threads (pane output, resize, user-var-changed) and a single dispatcher thread, verify that no events are lost under concurrent fire, that handler execution order is deterministic within a priority level, and that register/unregister operations concurrent with fire_event never cause use-after-free or missed handlers

## Cross-references
- **wa-1sm78** (lock-free data structures): The EventBus native handler dispatch should use the lock-free queue and concurrent map primitives from wa-1sm78 to achieve zero-contention event dispatch in the hot path — this is critical for the <1μs native dispatch target

title: Implement LuaEngine — ScriptingEngine wrapper for existing mlua code
description:
# Implement LuaEngine (ScriptingEngine trait wrapper for existing mlua code)

## Why
The existing Lua code in frankenterm/config/src/lua.rs and frankenterm/luahelper/ already works. We wrap it in the ScriptingEngine trait so it becomes one of multiple engines, not THE engine.

## What to build
1. `LuaEngine` struct implementing `ScriptingEngine` trait
2. Wraps existing `mlua::Lua` instance
3. `eval_config()` calls existing `load_configuration()` from lua.rs
4. `register_hook()` wraps Lua callback registration
5. `fire_event()` calls into Lua event handler tables
6. `load_extension()` loads Lua scripts as extensions
7. `capabilities()` returns: async=true, filesystem=true, network=true, sandboxed=false

## Key insight: minimal refactoring
We're NOT rewriting the Lua code. We're wrapping it. The existing lua.rs stays mostly as-is. LuaEngine is a thin adapter layer that maps ScriptingEngine methods to existing Lua functions.

## Files
- frankenterm/scripting/src/lua_engine.rs (NEW — adapter)
- frankenterm/scripting/Cargo.toml (optional dep on mlua, luahelper)
- frankenterm/config/src/lua.rs (minor: expose internal functions as pub(crate))

## Feature gating
```toml
[features]
lua = ["dep:mlua", "dep:luahelper"]
```
The entire LuaEngine module is behind `#[cfg(feature = "lua")]`.

## Testing
- Load a wezterm.lua config through LuaEngine.eval_config()
- Register and fire a Lua event hook
- Verify LuaEngine reports correct capabilities
- Backward compat: existing config loading behavior unchanged
- **criterion benchmarks**: Measure Lua script execution latency — benchmark eval_config() with a representative wezterm.lua config, fire_event() round-trip for a simple hook, and register_hook() throughput; establish baseline latencies for comparison with WasmEngine (wa-3dfxb.4)
- **proptest**: Property-based tests for Lua value conversion roundtrips — generate arbitrary Rust values (strings, integers, floats, booleans, nested tables/vecs), convert to mlua::Value and back, verify lossless roundtrip for all supported types

## Cross-references
- **wa-ggw9w**: Make Lua optional in config crate — LuaEngine must be fully behind the `lua` feature flag established by that bead

## Considerations
- LuaJIT is NOT Send (mlua handles this with userdata). LuaEngine must be Send+Sync as required by the trait — mlua's `send` feature handles this.
- Memory: Lua GC should be triggered periodically. Consider adding a `gc()` method to ScriptingEngine trait or handling it in LuaEngine internals.
- Error mapping: mlua::Error → anyhow::Error (already works via Into)

title: Add wasmtime + WASI integration to FrankenTerm workspace
description:
# Add wasmtime + WASI Integration to FrankenTerm Workspace

## Why
wasmtime is the WASM runtime for FrankenTerm's extension system. This bead adds it to the workspace and sets up the foundation.

## Why wasmtime specifically
- **Rust-native**: Written in Rust, by Bytecode Alliance (Mozilla, Fastly, Intel)
- **Proven**: Used by Zellij for terminal plugins, Fermyon Spin, Fastly Compute
- **WASI support**: Full WASI preview 1, Component Model for preview 2
- **Size**: ~5MB binary overhead (vs ~30MB for V8)
- **Security**: Sandboxed by default, capability-based, memory-safe
- **Performance**: Cranelift JIT compiler, competitive with native

## What to add

### Workspace dependencies (root Cargo.toml)
```toml
[workspace.dependencies]
wasmtime = { version = "28", default-features = false, features = ["cranelift", "async", "component-model"] }
wasmtime-wasi = { version = "28", default-features = false }
```

### frankenterm/scripting/Cargo.toml
```toml
[features]
wasm = ["dep:wasmtime", "dep:wasmtime-wasi"]

[dependencies]
wasmtime = { workspace = true, optional = true }
wasmtime-wasi = { workspace = true, optional = true }
```

## Version choice: wasmtime 28.x
- Latest stable as of early 2026
- Component Model stable
- WASI preview 2 support
- async support for non-blocking extension calls

## Build time impact
- wasmtime ~15s clean compile (pure Rust, parallelizes)
- Only compiled when `wasm` feature enabled
- Incremental: <2s (Cranelift changes rarely)

## Feature flag propagation
The `wasm` feature needs to propagate through:
- frankenterm/scripting (owns wasmtime dep)
- frankenterm/config (optional: WASM config evaluation)
- frankenterm/mux (optional: WASM plugin panes, future)
- wa-core (feature flag: `frankenterm-wasm`)
- wa (CLI feature flag: `wasm`)

## Testing
- `cargo check -p scripting --features wasm` compiles
- `cargo check` (default, no wasm) doesn't pull wasmtime
- Simple "hello world" WASM module loads and runs
- WASI stdio/env access works
- **criterion benchmarks**: Measure WASM module compilation time — benchmark wasmtime::Module::new() for small (1KB), medium (100KB), and large (1MB) WASM modules; track compilation latency to establish baselines and detect regressions when upgrading wasmtime versions

## Cross-references
- **wa-1pygr** (Zellij WASM plugin analysis): Zellij's wasmtime integration provides reference patterns for WASI configuration, module caching strategy, and host function binding — lessons learned there directly inform our wasmtime setup

## Considerations
- wasmtime's cranelift JIT requires a few seconds to compile WASM on first load. Consider caching compiled modules in ~/.cache/frankenterm/wasm/
- Memory limit: set wasmtime Store memory limit to prevent runaway extensions (default: 64MB per extension)
- Fuel metering: enable wasmtime fuel to prevent infinite loops (default: 1B instructions per call)

title: Implement WasmEngine — ScriptingEngine trait impl for wasmtime
description:
# Implement WasmEngine (ScriptingEngine trait impl for wasmtime)

## Why
This is the WASM side of the dual-runtime strategy. WasmEngine wraps wasmtime to provide sandboxed, polyglot extension execution.

## Architecture

### WasmEngine struct
```rust
pub struct WasmEngine {
    engine: wasmtime::Engine,
    linker: wasmtime::Linker<HostState>,
    module_cache: HashMap<PathBuf, wasmtime::Module>,
    extensions: HashMap<ExtensionId, LoadedExtension>,
    config: WasmEngineConfig,
}

struct HostState {
    wasi: WasiCtx,
    host_fns: FrankenTermHostFunctions,
    fuel_limit: u64,
    memory_limit: usize,
}

struct WasmEngineConfig {
    fuel_limit: u64,         // Default: 1_000_000_000 (1B instructions)
    memory_limit_mb: usize,  // Default: 64MB per extension
    cache_compiled: bool,    // Default: true, cache to disk
    cache_dir: PathBuf,      // Default: ~/.cache/frankenterm/wasm/
    allowed_dirs: Vec<PathBuf>,  // WASI filesystem access (empty = none)
}
```

### ScriptingEngine implementation
- `eval_config()`: Load .wasm config module, call `configure()` export, deserialize result
- `register_hook()`: Register WASM function as event hook (stored in host state)
- `fire_event()`: Serialize event payload → call WASM hook functions → deserialize actions
- `load_extension()`: Compile + instantiate WASM module, validate exports, register hooks
- `capabilities()`: async=true, filesystem=configurable, network=false, sandboxed=true

### Module caching
WASM compilation is slow (~seconds). Cache compiled modules:
```
~/.cache/frankenterm/wasm/
  <sha256_of_wasm_bytes>.cwasm   # Cranelift precompiled
```
Second load is instant (mmap the precompiled module).

## Host functions (FrankenTerm API)
WASM extensions can call these host functions:
```
ft_log(level: i32, msg_ptr: i32, msg_len: i32)
ft_get_config(key_ptr: i32, key_len: i32) -> i32
ft_set_config(key_ptr: i32, key_len: i32, val_ptr: i32, val_len: i32)
ft_register_hook(event_ptr: i32, event_len: i32, func_idx: i32) -> i32
ft_get_pane_text(pane_id: i32, lines: i32) -> i32
ft_send_input(pane_id: i32, text_ptr: i32, text_len: i32)
ft_get_env(key_ptr: i32, key_len: i32) -> i32
```
These are defined via wasmtime's `Linker::func_wrap()`.

## Component Model (future)
wasmtime's Component Model allows structured types (records, variants, lists) instead of raw pointers. This is the future direction — start with core WASM (raw pointers + serde), migrate to Component Model once WIT tooling matures.

## Files
- frankenterm/scripting/src/wasm_engine.rs (NEW — main impl)
- frankenterm/scripting/src/wasm_host.rs (NEW — host function definitions)
- frankenterm/scripting/src/wasm_cache.rs (NEW — module caching)
- frankenterm/scripting/src/wasm_types.rs (NEW — serialization helpers)

## Testing
- Load a simple WASM extension and verify it runs
- Test fuel metering (infinite loop gets killed)
- Test memory limits (allocating too much gets killed)
- Test host function calls (log, get_config, etc.)
- Test module caching (second load is instant)
- Benchmark: extension call overhead (target: <100μs per call)
- **criterion benchmarks**: Measure WASM execution latency end-to-end — benchmark fire_event() roundtrip (host → WASM → host), eval_config() for a WASM config module, and load_extension() cold vs cached; compare directly with LuaEngine (wa-3dfxb.2) benchmarks to validate the <100μs target and quantify the Lua-vs-WASM tradeoff
- **proptest**: Property-based tests for WASM value conversion roundtrips — generate arbitrary Rust values, serialize to WASM linear memory format, call a WASM echo function, deserialize the result, and verify lossless roundtrip for all supported types (integers, floats, strings, byte arrays, nested structures)
- **LabRuntime DPOR**: Model concurrent WASM execution with LabRuntime's dynamic partial-order reduction — verify that multiple extensions firing events concurrently on separate Stores never observe torn state in shared host data (config values, hook registrations), and that fuel exhaustion in one extension does not corrupt another's execution state

## Considerations
- wasmtime Store is not Send — each thread needs its own Store. For async, use wasmtime's async support with one Store per task.
- Extension isolation: each extension gets its own Store+memory. One crashing extension can't affect others.
- Startup time: first-time compilation is ~1-3s per extension. Module cache makes subsequent loads instant.

title: WASM extension sandbox security model
description:
# WASM Extension Sandbox Security Model

## Why
WASM extensions run user-supplied code inside FrankenTerm. The sandbox must prevent malicious or buggy extensions from: (1) crashing the host, (2) consuming unbounded resources, (3) accessing unauthorized files/network, (4) interfering with other extensions.

## Security layers

### Layer 1: WASM memory isolation (built-in)
Each WASM module gets its own linear memory. It cannot access host memory, other extensions' memory, or any memory outside its sandbox. This is a fundamental WASM guarantee.

### Layer 2: Capability-based WASI access
Extensions declare required capabilities in their manifest:
```toml
[permissions]
filesystem = ["read:~/.config/frankenterm/", "write:~/.local/share/frankenterm/"]
environment = ["TERM", "COLORTERM", "FRANKENTERM_*"]
network = false  # No network access for v1
```
The WasmEngine configures WASI to only expose what's declared. Undeclared capabilities are denied at the WASI layer.

### Layer 3: Fuel metering (CPU limits)
wasmtime's fuel system counts instructions. Default: 1 billion fuel per event handler call. If exhausted, the call is terminated with an error. Prevents infinite loops and CPU hogging.

### Layer 4: Memory limits
wasmtime Store has a `limiter()` API. Default: 64MB per extension. If exceeded, memory allocation traps. Prevents memory bombs.

### Layer 5: Host function auditing
Every host function call is logged to an audit trail:
```
[2026-02-10T12:00:00Z] ext:my-theme ft_get_config("color_scheme") -> ok
[2026-02-10T12:00:00Z] ext:my-theme ft_set_config("cursor_style", "block") -> ok
[2026-02-10T12:00:01Z] ext:sketchy ft_get_pane_text(0, 1000) -> denied(no_pane_access)
```

### Layer 6: Extension signing (future, v2)
Extensions can be signed with ed25519 keys. FrankenTerm can be configured to only load signed extensions. Not in v1 scope but the manifest format reserves fields for it.

## Manifest format (extension.toml)
```toml
[extension]
name = "my-theme"
version = "1.0.0"
description = "A beautiful theme for FrankenTerm"
authors = ["Author Name <author@example.com>"]
license = "MIT"
min_frankenterm_version = "0.2.0"

[permissions]
filesystem = []
environment = ["TERM", "COLORTERM"]
network = false
pane_access = false  # Can't read/write pane content

[hooks]
on_config_reload = "handle_config_reload"
on_pane_focus = "handle_pane_focus"

# Future
[signing]
algorithm = "ed25519"
# signature in separate .sig file
```

## Threat model
| Threat | Mitigation |
|--------|------------|
| Infinite loop | Fuel metering, 1B instruction limit |
| Memory bomb | 64MB per-extension limit |
| Filesystem access | WASI capability scoping |
| Network exfiltration | Network disabled by default |
| Host crash | WASM isolation, error boundaries |
| Cross-extension attack | Separate Stores, no shared memory |
| Supply chain | Signing (v2), capability audit trail |

## Files
- frankenterm/scripting/src/sandbox.rs (NEW — sandbox configuration)
- frankenterm/scripting/src/manifest.rs (NEW — extension.toml parsing)
- frankenterm/scripting/src/audit.rs (NEW — host function audit trail)

## Testing
- Test that an extension without filesystem permission can't read files
- Test that fuel exhaustion terminates cleanly (no host crash)
- Test that memory limit triggers clean trap
- Test audit trail records all host function calls
- Test malicious WASM module (crafted to exploit) is safely contained
- Fuzz: random WASM bytes don't crash the host (wasmtime validates)
- **proptest**: Property-based tests for sandbox escape invariants — generate random combinations of permission sets and host function call sequences, verify that every call without the required permission is denied, that no sequence of allowed calls can escalate to undeclared permissions, and that sandbox state remains consistent after denied calls
- **criterion benchmarks**: Measure sandbox enforcement overhead — benchmark the cost of permission checks on each host function call (target: <50ns per check), audit trail logging overhead (must not exceed 1% of total call time), and fuel metering overhead vs unmetered execution

## Cross-references
- **wa-1pygr** (Zellij WASM plugin analysis): Zellij's sandbox model and permission system provide direct prior art — their capability-based WASI configuration patterns and lessons learned from real-world plugin sandboxing inform our security layer design

title: Config format auto-detection and multi-format loading
description:
# Config Format Auto-Detection and Multi-Format Loading

## Why
FrankenTerm supports three config formats: wezterm.lua (legacy), frankenterm.toml (default), and frankenterm.wasm (dynamic). The config loader must auto-detect which format is present and load accordingly.

## Detection priority
When no config path is specified explicitly:
1. Look for `frankenterm.toml` in standard locations
2. Look for `frankenterm.wasm` in standard locations (if `wasm` feature enabled)
3. Look for `wezterm.lua` or `.wezterm.lua` in standard locations (if `lua` feature enabled)
4. Fall back to built-in defaults

### Standard locations (in order)
- `$FRANKENTERM_CONFIG_FILE` (explicit override)
- `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/frankenterm/frankenterm.toml`
- `~/.config/frankenterm/frankenterm.toml`
- `~/.wezterm.lua` (legacy compat)
- `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/wezterm/wezterm.lua` (legacy compat)

## macOS fallbacks
On macOS, also check Application Support paths in addition to XDG locations:
- `~/Library/Application Support/FrankenTerm/frankenterm.toml`
- `~/Library/Application Support/FrankenTerm/frankenterm.wasm`

The detection order prefers XDG paths (for cross-platform consistency) but falls back to macOS-native paths when XDG locations are empty.

## Implementation
```rust
pub enum ConfigFormat {
    Toml,
    Lua,
    Wasm,
    Default,  // No config file found, use built-in defaults
}

pub fn detect_config() -> (ConfigFormat, Option<PathBuf>) {
    // Check explicit env var first
    // Then probe standard locations in priority order
    // Return format + path
}

pub fn load_config(format: ConfigFormat, path: Option<&Path>, dispatcher: &ScriptingDispatcher) -> Result<TerminalConfiguration> {
    match format {
        ConfigFormat::Toml => load_toml_config(path.unwrap()),
        ConfigFormat::Lua => dispatcher.eval_config_with_engine("lua", path.unwrap()),
        ConfigFormat::Wasm => dispatcher.eval_config_with_engine("wasm", path.unwrap()),
        ConfigFormat::Default => Ok(TerminalConfiguration::default()),
    }
}
```

## User communication
On startup, log which config format was detected:
```
[INFO] Config: loaded frankenterm.toml from ~/.config/frankenterm/
[INFO] Config: loaded wezterm.lua (legacy) from ~/.wezterm.lua
[WARN] Config: no config file found, using defaults
```

## Files
- frankenterm/config/src/detection.rs (NEW — format detection logic)
- frankenterm/config/src/loader.rs (NEW or modify existing — multi-format dispatcher)

## Testing
- Test each format is correctly detected from standard locations
- Test priority: frankenterm.toml wins over wezterm.lua
- Test explicit $FRANKENTERM_CONFIG_FILE overrides everything
- Test graceful fallback to defaults when no config exists
- Test error messages for malformed config of each type
- **proptest**: Property-based tests for format detection correctness — generate random filesystem layouts with combinations of Lua, TOML, and WASM config files present at various standard locations, verify that the detection algorithm always selects the correct format according to the priority rules and never misidentifies a file format based on extension or content
- **criterion benchmarks**: Measure detection latency — benchmark the full detect_config() probe sequence (filesystem stat calls for all standard locations) to ensure detection completes in <1ms even when probing many paths; also benchmark load_config() per-format to track loader overhead

## Cross-references
- **wa-2t4oa** (structured config format): The TOML config schema and loading logic defined there is the primary config path that this auto-detection feeds into — detection must be compatible with the TOML schema versioning defined in wa-2t4oa

title: wezterm.lua to frankenterm.toml migration tool
description:
# wezterm.lua → frankenterm.toml Migration Tool

## Why
Users migrating from WezTerm have existing wezterm.lua configs. We need a best-effort migration tool that converts Lua configs to TOML format.

## Scope: best-effort
Lua configs can contain arbitrary code (functions, conditionals, loops). We can't convert arbitrary Lua to TOML. What we CAN convert:
- Static assignments: `config.font_size = 14` → `font_size = 14`
- Color scheme references: `config.color_scheme = "Dracula"` → `color_scheme = "Dracula"`
- Simple key bindings: `config.keys = { {key="c", mods="CTRL", action=wezterm.action.Copy} }`
- SSH domains: static domain definitions
- String/number/boolean config values

What we CANNOT convert (user must port manually or use WASM):
- Dynamic configs: `if hostname == "work" then ... end`
- Custom functions: `wezterm.on("update-status", function(...) ... end)`
- Complex Lua tables with computed keys
- Plugin references

## Implementation approach
Two strategies, used together:
1. **AST parsing**: Use a Lua parser (full_moon or similar) to parse the Lua AST and extract simple assignments. This handles ~70% of configs.
2. **Runtime extraction**: Actually run the Lua config with mlua, capture the resulting config table, and serialize it to TOML. This handles dynamic configs but requires the `lua` feature.

## CLI command
```bash
# Convert wezterm.lua to frankenterm.toml
frankenterm migrate-config ~/.wezterm.lua -o ~/.config/frankenterm/frankenterm.toml

# Dry run (show what would be generated)
frankenterm migrate-config ~/.wezterm.lua --dry-run

# Verbose (show what couldn't be converted)
frankenterm migrate-config ~/.wezterm.lua --verbose
```

## Output format
```toml
# Migrated from ~/.wezterm.lua on 2026-02-10
# Some settings could not be automatically converted.
# See comments marked [MANUAL] below.

font_size = 14.0
color_scheme = "Dracula"

[keys]
# [MANUAL] Complex key binding with custom action — review manually:
# Original Lua: wezterm.action_callback(function(window, pane) ... end)

[ssh_domains]
[[ssh_domains.domains]]
name = "work"
remote_address = "work.example.com"
```

## Files
- frankenterm/config/src/migrate.rs (NEW — migration logic)
- Or: standalone binary frankenterm-migrate (if we want it separate)

## Testing
- Convert 10 representative wezterm.lua configs (from WezTerm docs examples)
- Verify round-trip: load original Lua, load migrated TOML, compare config values
- Test unconvertible constructs produce clear [MANUAL] comments
- Test --dry-run doesn't write files
- Test --verbose shows all unconverted items
- **proptest**: Property-based tests for migration roundtrip fidelity — generate random valid Lua config tables with known static assignments (font_size, color_scheme, boolean flags, string values, simple key bindings), migrate to TOML, parse the TOML back, and verify every convertible field matches the original Lua value; also verify that unconvertible constructs always produce [MANUAL] annotations rather than silent data loss

## Cross-references
- **wa-vv3h** (rename project): The migration tool must use the post-rename binary name and config paths — coordinate naming so that `frankenterm migrate-config` is the canonical invocation and output paths default to frankenterm.toml (not wezterm.toml)

title: FrankenTerm Extension Package Format (.ftx)
description:
# FrankenTerm Extension Package Format (.ftx)

## Why
Extensions need a standard packaging format for distribution, installation, and loading. The .ftx format bundles everything an extension needs.

## Format specification

### .ftx file structure
A .ftx file is a ZIP archive with this structure:
```
my-extension.ftx (ZIP)
├── extension.toml          # Manifest (required)
├── main.wasm               # WASM module (required for WASM extensions)
├── main.lua                # Lua script (required for Lua extensions)
├── assets/                 # Optional: themes, icons, etc.
│   ├── theme.toml
│   └── icon.png
├── README.md               # Optional: documentation
└── LICENSE                  # Optional: license file
```

### extension.toml (manifest)
```toml
[extension]
name = "my-theme"
version = "1.0.0"
description = "A beautiful theme"
authors = ["Author <author@example.com>"]
license = "MIT"
homepage = "https://github.com/author/my-theme"
min_frankenterm_version = "0.2.0"

[engine]
type = "wasm"  # or "lua" or "both"
entry = "main.wasm"  # or "main.lua"

[permissions]
filesystem = []
environment = ["TERM"]
network = false
pane_access = false

[hooks]
on_config_reload = "handle_config_reload"
on_pane_focus = "handle_pane_focus"
on_color_scheme_change = "handle_color_scheme"

[assets]
themes = ["assets/theme.toml"]
```

### Extension types
1. **Theme extensions**: Color scheme + font config, no code needed (just TOML assets)
2. **Hook extensions**: React to events (config reload, pane focus, etc.)
3. **Content extensions**: Provide pane content (status bars, clocks, etc.) — future
4. **Transform extensions**: Modify terminal output (syntax highlighting, etc.) — future

## Loading and installation
```bash
# Install from file
frankenterm extension install my-theme.ftx

# Install from URL (future)
frankenterm extension install https://example.com/my-theme.ftx

# List installed
frankenterm extension list

# Remove
frankenterm extension remove my-theme

# Extension directory
~/.local/share/frankenterm/extensions/
  my-theme/
    extension.toml
    main.wasm
    assets/
```

## macOS fallbacks
On macOS, the default extension directory also checks:
- `~/Library/Application Support/FrankenTerm/extensions/`
Prefer XDG paths when set, but fall back to macOS-native Application Support when XDG_DATA_HOME is unset.

## Implementation
- Parse extension.toml using existing toml workspace dep
- Validate WASM module exports match declared hooks
- Validate permissions are minimal (warn on excessive permissions)
- Cache compiled WASM modules per extension version

## Files
- frankenterm/scripting/src/extension.rs (NEW — extension loading)
- frankenterm/scripting/src/manifest.rs (NEW — extension.toml parsing)
- frankenterm/scripting/src/package.rs (NEW — .ftx ZIP handling)

## Dependencies
- zip = "2" (for .ftx reading) — add to workspace
- Already have: toml, serde, anyhow

## Testing
- Create a minimal .ftx with just manifest + WASM
- Load and verify manifest parsing
- Load and instantiate WASM module from .ftx
- Test invalid manifests are rejected with clear errors
- Test permission validation
- Test extension install/list/remove CLI commands
- **proptest**: Property-based tests for package manifest parsing — generate random valid and invalid extension.toml manifests (varying field combinations, version strings, permission sets, hook declarations), verify that valid manifests parse correctly and all fields roundtrip through serialize/deserialize, and that invalid manifests produce clear error messages rather than panics
- **criterion benchmarks**: Measure package loading performance — benchmark .ftx ZIP extraction time for packages of varying sizes (1KB theme-only to 5MB WASM+assets), manifest parsing latency, and full load_extension() pipeline including WASM compilation; establish baselines for extension marketplace responsiveness

title: Extension API: keybindings, events, pane hooks, storage
description:
# FrankenTerm Extension API: Keybindings, Events, Pane Hooks

## Why
Extensions need a rich API to be useful. This bead defines the host functions, event system, and hooks that extensions can use.

## Event system

### Built-in events (extensions can hook into)
| Event | Payload | When |
|-------|---------|------|
| `config.reload` | `{path: String}` | Config file changed |
| `pane.focus` | `{pane_id: u32, prev: u32}` | Pane focus changed |
| `pane.created` | `{pane_id: u32, domain: String}` | New pane opened |
| `pane.closed` | `{pane_id: u32}` | Pane closed |
| `pane.output` | `{pane_id: u32, text: String}` | New output (throttled) |
| `pane.title_changed` | `{pane_id: u32, title: String}` | Pane title changed |
| `tab.created` | `{tab_id: u32}` | New tab created |
| `tab.closed` | `{tab_id: u32}` | Tab closed |
| `window.focus` | `{window_id: u32}` | Window focus changed |
| `key.pressed` | `{key: String, mods: String}` | Key press (if not consumed by binding) |
| `session.save` | `{path: String}` | Session being saved |
| `session.restore` | `{path: String}` | Session being restored |

### Custom events (extensions can fire)
Extensions can fire custom events that other extensions can hook:
```
ft_fire_event("my-extension.custom-event", payload_ptr, payload_len)
```

## Host function API (WASM)

### Core functions
```
// Logging
ft_log(level: i32, msg_ptr: i32, msg_len: i32)

// Config access (read-only for most extensions)
ft_get_config(key_ptr: i32, key_len: i32, out_ptr: i32, out_len: i32) -> i32
ft_set_config(key_ptr: i32, key_len: i32, val_ptr: i32, val_len: i32) -> i32

// Pane interaction (requires pane_access permission)
ft_get_pane_text(pane_id: i32, lines: i32, out_ptr: i32, out_len: i32) -> i32
ft_send_input(pane_id: i32, text_ptr: i32, text_len: i32) -> i32
ft_get_pane_info(pane_id: i32, out_ptr: i32, out_len: i32) -> i32
ft_list_panes(out_ptr: i32, out_len: i32) -> i32

// Event system
ft_register_hook(event_ptr: i32, event_len: i32, priority: i32, func_name_ptr: i32, func_name_len: i32) -> i32
ft_fire_event(event_ptr: i32, event_len: i32, payload_ptr: i32, payload_len: i32) -> i32

// Keybinding
ft_register_keybinding(key_ptr: i32, key_len: i32, mods: i32, func_name_ptr: i32, func_name_len: i32) -> i32

// Environment (requires environment permission)
ft_get_env(key_ptr: i32, key_len: i32, out_ptr: i32, out_len: i32) -> i32

// Timer (async callback after delay)
ft_set_timeout(ms: i32, func_name_ptr: i32, func_name_len: i32) -> i32
ft_set_interval(ms: i32, func_name_ptr: i32, func_name_len: i32) -> i32
ft_clear_timer(timer_id: i32)

// Extension storage (per-extension key-value store)
ft_storage_get(key_ptr: i32, key_len: i32, out_ptr: i32, out_len: i32) -> i32
ft_storage_set(key_ptr: i32, key_len: i32, val_ptr: i32, val_len: i32) -> i32
```

## Lua API (equivalent)
The Lua engine exposes equivalent APIs through Lua tables:
```lua
frankenterm.log("info", "Hello from extension")
frankenterm.get_config("font_size")
frankenterm.on("pane.focus", function(event) ... end)
frankenterm.register_keybinding("ctrl+shift+t", function() ... end)
```

## Extension SDK (for WASM extension authors)
Provide a Rust crate `frankenterm-extension-sdk` that wraps raw host functions:
```rust
use frankenterm_extension_sdk::*;

#[ft_hook("pane.focus")]
fn on_pane_focus(event: PaneFocusEvent) -> Result<()> {
    ft::log::info!("Pane {} focused", event.pane_id);
    Ok(())
}

#[ft_hook("config.reload")]  
fn on_config_reload(event: ConfigReloadEvent) -> Result<()> {
    let theme = ft::config::get("color_scheme")?;
    ft::log::info!("Config reloaded, theme: {}", theme);
    Ok(())
}
```

## Files
- frankenterm/scripting/src/host_api.rs (NEW — host function implementations)
- frankenterm/scripting/src/events.rs (NEW — event system)
- frankenterm/scripting/src/keybindings.rs (NEW — keybinding registration)
- frankenterm/scripting/src/storage.rs (NEW — per-extension KV store)
- frankenterm-extension-sdk/ (NEW crate — Rust SDK for extension authors)

## Testing
- Test each host function individually
- Test event dispatch through extensions
- Test keybinding registration and triggering
- Test extension storage persistence
- Test permission enforcement (pane_access denied → ft_get_pane_text fails)
- Test timer/interval scheduling
- End-to-end: load an extension that registers a keybinding and fires on keypress
- **criterion benchmarks**: Measure event dispatch latency — benchmark fire_event() for each built-in event type with 1, 10, and 50 registered hooks, measure ft_register_hook() and ft_register_keybinding() registration throughput, and benchmark ft_storage_get/set latency; target <50μs for single-hook event dispatch and <500μs for 50-hook fan-out
- **proptest**: Property-based tests for event ordering — generate random sequences of hook registrations with varying priorities, fire events, and verify that hooks always execute in priority order; also generate interleaved register/unregister/fire sequences and verify no hooks are called after unregistration and no events are lost
- **LabRuntime DPOR**: Model concurrent hook execution with LabRuntime's dynamic partial-order reduction — verify that concurrent event dispatch (multiple events fired simultaneously from different panes) correctly serializes hook execution per-extension while allowing cross-extension parallelism, and that timer callbacks interleaved with event dispatch maintain consistent extension state

title: [EPIC] Performance Optimizations: Lazy Loading, Caching, Pooling
description:
# [EPIC] Performance Optimizations

## Mission
Make wa **fast and efficient** without sacrificing safety or correctness.

## Why This Matters
wa runs continuously in the background. Performance impacts:
- CPU usage (battery life on laptops)
- Memory footprint
- Latency of operations
- Scalability to many panes

Optimizations must be:
- Measurable (benchmarks prove value)
- Safe (no correctness regressions)
- Conditional (only apply when beneficial)

## Components

### 1. Lazy Pattern Compilation
Do not compile regex/Aho-Corasick engines until first use:
```rust
static PATTERN_ENGINE: Lazy<PatternEngine> = Lazy::new(|| {
    PatternEngine::compile(load_packs())
});
```

Benefits:
- Faster startup time
- Memory saved if patterns not used
- Hot-reload ready

### 2. Bloom Filter Pre-Filter
Before running Aho-Corasick, check Bloom filter:
```rust
if !bloom_filter.possibly_contains(&text) {
    return vec![]; // Quick reject
}
// Only then run full pattern matching
```

Budget: < 1µs for Bloom check

### 3. Connection Pooling for WezTerm CLI
Keep warm connections to WezTerm mux server:
```rust
struct WezTermPool {
    connections: Vec<MuxConnection>,
    max_size: usize,
}
```

Benefits:
- Avoid process spawn overhead
- Reduce socket churn
- Enable connection reuse

Note: Only beneficial if vendored mode or mux protocol direct access.

### 4. Memory-Efficient Output Cache
Already exists as `wa-4vx.4.12` - enhance with:
- LRU eviction by memory pressure
- Rolling hash for dedup detection
- Configurable cache size limits

### 5. Background Segment Compression
Already gated by `wa-4vx.3.11` decision - if needed:
- Compress segments older than N days
- Use zstd for good ratio and speed
- Transparent decompression on read
- Background compaction thread

### 6. Incremental FTS Sync
Ensure FTS index only processes new content:
- Track last-indexed segment per pane
- Batch index updates
- Avoid full reindex on restart

## Benchmarks
All optimizations must be validated by Criterion benchmarks:
- Baseline before optimization
- Result after optimization
- Regression tests to prevent backsliding

## Testing
- Benchmark suite for each optimization
- Memory profiling under sustained load
- No correctness regressions (same outputs)

## Success Criteria
- Startup time < 100ms (no feature flags)
- Pattern quick-reject < 1µs for non-matching text
- Memory usage < 100MB for typical workload
- CPU usage < 5% when idle

## Acceptance Criteria
- Each optimization yields measurable latency or memory improvement.
- Performance budgets are enforced in CI.
- Regression thresholds and baselines are documented.

title: Bloom filter pre-filter: quick reject non-matching text before regex
description:
# Bloom Filter Pre-Filter

## Purpose
Use a Bloom filter to quickly reject text that definitely doesn't match any pattern, avoiding expensive regex evaluation.

## How It Works
1. Build Bloom filter from all pattern keywords
2. For each incoming text segment:
   a. Hash key substrings through Bloom filter
   b. If Bloom returns "definitely not present" → skip
   c. Only if Bloom says "possibly present" → run full patterns

## Implementation
```rust
use bloomfilter::Bloom;

pub struct PatternEngine {
    bloom: Bloom<str>,          // Quick reject filter
    aho_corasick: AhoCorasick,  // Actual pattern matcher
}

impl PatternEngine {
    pub fn matches(&self, text: &str) -> Vec<Match> {
        // Quick reject: < 1µs
        if !self.bloom_possibly_contains(text) {
            return vec![];
        }
        // Full match: ~10-100µs
        self.aho_corasick_match(text)
    }
}
```

## Bloom Filter Parameters
- Size: ~10KB for 1000 patterns
- False positive rate: ~1%
- Hash functions: 3

## Benchmark Targets
- Bloom check: < 1µs
- Typical text (no matches): ~1µs total
- Text with matches: ~10-100µs (unchanged)
- 90%+ of segments rejected by Bloom

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Bloom filter built from pattern keywords
- [ ] Quick reject path < 1µs
- [ ] False positive rate verified < 5%
- [ ] Benchmark shows improvement for non-matching text

## Testing
- Criterion benchmarks with budgets and baseline comparison.
- Microbenchmarks for the specific optimization.
- CI regression guard with perf logs.

title: Connection pooling for WezTerm: reuse mux connections when available
description:
# Connection Pooling for WezTerm

## Purpose
Reduce overhead of WezTerm CLI calls by pooling connections to the mux server.

## Current Behavior
Each WezTerm CLI call spawns a new process, connects to mux, executes, and disconnects.

## Proposed Behavior
When using vendored mode (direct mux protocol):
```rust
pub struct WezTermPool {
    connections: Vec<MuxConnection>,
    max_size: usize,
    idle_timeout: Duration,
}

impl WezTermPool {
    pub async fn execute<T>(&self, cmd: MuxCommand) -> Result<T> {
        let conn = self.acquire().await?;
        let result = conn.execute(cmd).await;
        self.release(conn);
        result
    }
}
```

## Benefits
- Avoid process spawn overhead (~10ms per call)
- Reduce socket churn
- Enable connection keepalive
- Batch multiple operations efficiently

## Prerequisites
- Requires vendored mode (wa-nu4.4.1)
- Direct mux protocol access

## Fallback
CLI mode: No pooling possible, but can batch commands.

## Benchmark Targets
- With pooling: ~1ms per operation
- Without pooling: ~10-20ms per operation
- 10x improvement for high-frequency operations

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Connection pool implemented for vendored mode
- [ ] Idle connection cleanup
- [ ] Graceful fallback for CLI mode
- [ ] Benchmark proves improvement

## Testing
- Criterion benchmarks with budgets and baseline comparison.
- Microbenchmarks for the specific optimization.
- CI regression guard with perf logs.

title: Incremental FTS sync: avoid full reindex, track per-pane progress
description:
# Incremental FTS Sync

## Purpose
Ensure FTS index only processes new content, avoiding expensive full reindex operations.

## Current Challenge
On restart, wa might need to determine what's already indexed and what's new.

## Solution
```rust
pub struct FtsIndexState {
    /// Last indexed segment seq per pane
    per_pane_progress: HashMap<PaneId, SegmentSeq>,
    /// Global index version for schema changes
    index_version: u32,
}
```

## Sync Process
1. On startup: Load `per_pane_progress` from DB
2. For each pane: Query segments where `seq > last_indexed_seq`
3. Index only new segments
4. Update progress after successful batch

## Batching Strategy
- Batch size: 100 segments or 1MB text
- Commit progress after each batch
- Resume from last batch on crash

## Performance Impact
- Full reindex: O(total segments)
- Incremental: O(new segments)
- Startup overhead: O(1) - just load progress

## Recovery
If index corrupt or schema changed:
- Detect via `index_version` mismatch
- Trigger full rebuild
- Show progress indicator

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Per-pane progress tracked in DB
- [ ] Only new segments indexed on restart
- [ ] Batch processing with progress commits
- [ ] Full rebuild triggered on version mismatch
- [ ] Benchmark shows startup improvement

## Testing
- Criterion benchmarks with budgets and baseline comparison.
- Microbenchmarks for the specific optimization.
- CI regression guard with perf logs.

All 10 new tests pass.

title: Performance benchmarks and budgets: Criterion suite with regression guards
description:
# Performance benchmarks and budgets (Criterion)

## Goal
Establish benchmarks for all performance-critical paths and prevent regressions with explicit, documented budgets.

This system sits on the hot path of “every command the user runs” (watch loop, pattern matching, policy checks). Performance regressions are user-visible.

## Benchmark suite (Criterion)
Benchmarks must target *real* hot paths and be runnable locally:

```rust
// benches/pattern_engine.rs
criterion_group!(
    pattern_benchmarks,
    bench_bloom_check,
    bench_aho_corasick_match,
    bench_full_pattern_pipeline,
);

// benches/ingest.rs
criterion_group!(
    ingest_benchmarks,
    bench_delta_extraction,
    bench_segment_persistence,
    bench_fts_indexing,
);
```

## What we benchmark (minimum set)
- Quick reject / prefilter:
  - `memchr`/bloom/no-match fast paths
  - worst-case “near match but reject” path
- Pattern pipeline:
  - no-hit text (must be very fast)
  - one-hit typical text
  - extraction path with captures
- Ingest/deltas:
  - delta extraction on typical scrollback
  - gap detection path
- Storage:
  - write queue throughput (bounded queue)
  - FTS indexing cost for typical segment sizes
- Query surfaces:
  - typical FTS query latency (scoped)
  - worst-case query guardrails (bounded)

## Performance budgets (absolute ceilings)
Budgets are set as “this must feel snappy to users” ceilings. Exact numbers may be tuned after first implementation, but budgets must exist before optimization work is called done.

| Operation | Budget (target ceiling) | Notes |
|-----------|--------------------------|-------|
| Bloom filter check | < 1µs | hot path prefilter |
| Pattern match (no hit) | < 10µs | must be cheap for most text |
| Pattern match (with hit) | < 100µs | includes extraction |
| Delta extraction | < 1ms | per pane per tick typical |
| FTS insert (single) | < 5ms | typical segment size |
| FTS query (typical) | < 50ms | scoped query; “feels instant” |
| Startup (no patterns) | < 100ms | CLI responsiveness |

## Regression detection strategy (CI realities)
Perf measurement is noisy on shared runners. The plan must be robust:

- Local dev loop:
  - `cargo bench` is the source of truth for tuning.
  - Provide a short “budget check” summary line per benchmark so developers can self-serve.

- CI loop (two-tier):
  1) **PR job (warn-only by default)**
     - Run benches and upload `criterion` output + a short summary artifact.
     - Fail only on catastrophic regressions (e.g., >2x slower OR exceeding a hard ceiling by a large margin).
  2) **Main/perf job (enforce budgets)**
     - Prefer a stable environment (self-hosted runner if available).
     - Enforce budgets strictly and record historical trend artifacts.

- Baselines:
  - Store a baseline artifact from main (or a tagged commit) and compare PR results against it.
  - Comparisons must ignore obviously-noisy fields and focus on timing deltas.

## Reporting
Example (desired UX):
```
$ cargo bench --bench pattern_engine

bloom_check         time:   [0.8 µs 0.9 µs 1.0 µs]  ✓ (budget: 1µs)
aho_corasick_match  time:   [8.2 µs 8.5 µs 8.8 µs]  ✓ (budget: 10µs)
full_pipeline       time:   [45 µs 48 µs 51 µs]     ✓ (budget: 100µs)
```

On regression, the report must include:
- which benchmark regressed
- old vs new timings
- which budget was exceeded (if any)
- where to find the artifacts (CI URL/path)

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Criterion benchmarks exist for the minimum hot paths listed above.
- [ ] Budgets are documented and checked by an automated “budget check” step.
- [ ] CI produces artifacts for every run (raw criterion + summarized results).
- [ ] CI regression detection works (warn-only on PR; enforced on stable perf job).

## Testing
- Benchmark harness self-checks:
  - benches compile and run on supported platforms.
  - the budget-checking logic is covered by unit tests (parsing/threshold evaluation).
- CI regression guard tests:
  - include a small synthetic “known regression” fixture in test mode to verify:
    - the budget checker fails when it should
    - output includes the expected summary fields

description:
# Unify TUI Stack for FrankenTerm Dashboard

## Skills: /idea-wizard, /extreme-software-optimization

## Available TUI libraries (all ours)
1. **charmed_rust** (bubbletea Elm architecture, lipgloss styling, 16+ widgets)
2. **frankentui** (minimal kernel, diff-based rendering, SIMD, inline mode)
3. **rich_rust** (output formatting, tables, panels, syntax highlighting)
4. **opentui_rust** (low-level foundation, deterministic rendering)

## Integration plan

### Architecture
- **frankentui** as the rendering kernel (diff-based, RAII cleanup, inline mode)
- **charmed_rust** widgets for interactive components (lists, tables, text input)
- **lipgloss** for consistent styling across all UI elements
- **rich_rust** for formatted output in non-interactive contexts (CLI, robot mode)

### Dashboard components
1. **Pane picker**: Browse active panes, filter by status/age/CPU, select to focus
2. **Event feed**: Real-time stream of pattern detections, workflow triggers, alerts
3. **Stats panel**: Live metrics — pane count, memory, CPU pressure, FD usage
4. **Cost tracker**: Per-provider spending, quota bars, rate limit alerts (from caut)
5. **Session history**: Recent cass search results, relevant past solutions
6. **Bead progress**: Current bead work items, dependency graph visualization

### Inline mode (killer feature)
FrankenTerm TUI uses frankentui's inline mode:
- Status bar at bottom: pane count, alerts, CPU/memory pressure
- Agent output scrolls above naturally
- UI chrome never disrupts scrollback

### Performance (/extreme-software-optimization)
- Rendering: <16ms per frame (60fps capable)
- Diff-based: only redraw changed cells
- SIMD: accelerated color computation and layout calculation

## Tests
- Visual regression tests for each dashboard component
- Performance: measure render time under 200-pane load
- Inline mode: verify scrollback not disrupted

## Acceptance criteria
- Dashboard renders all 6 components
- Inline mode works correctly
- <16ms render time per frame
- Consistent styling via lipgloss
- Graceful degradation on small terminals

## Test Framework Requirements
- **Criterion benchmarks**: TUI render frame time benchmarks targeting <16ms for 60fps:
  - Full dashboard render: benchmark rendering all 6 components with realistic data (200 panes, 50 events, 16 providers). Target <16ms per frame.
  - Diff-based render: benchmark incremental render when only 1 component changes. Target <2ms per frame.
  - Individual component render: benchmark each of the 6 components individually. Identify the most expensive component.
  - Terminal size scaling: benchmark render at 80x24, 120x40, 200x60 terminal sizes. Verify render time scales sub-linearly.
  - SIMD color computation: benchmark lipgloss color blending with and without SIMD. Verify >2x improvement.
- **Proptest for widget layout invariants**: Property-based tests for layout correctness:
  - Generate random terminal dimensions (width 20-300, height 10-100), verify all widgets fit within bounds (no overflow, no negative sizes)
  - Generate random data sizes (0 to 10000 items in lists, 0 to 200 panes), verify layout remains valid (no overlapping widgets, no gaps)
  - Generate random resize sequences, verify layout recalculation produces consistent results (same final size = same final layout, regardless of intermediate sizes)
  - For each widget: generate random content, verify the rendered output has the correct number of lines and columns (matches the allocated space)

## Cross-References
- **wa-3kxe.5** (Operational telemetry): The dashboard's stats panel displays telemetry data collected by the operational telemetry pipeline. The telemetry system produces histograms, counters, and resource metrics; the dashboard consumes and visualizes them. Coordinate the data format — the telemetry pipeline should emit data in a structure the dashboard can directly render without transformation.

# Make luahelper Crate Fully Optional

## Context (revised from "Remove luahelper dependency")
Under the dual-runtime strategy, luahelper stays in the tree but becomes optional. When the `lua` feature is disabled, no crate should depend on luahelper.

## Crates that currently depend on luahelper
1. config — for Lua config parsing → gate behind `lua` feature
2. mux — for Lua domain management → gate behind `lua` feature
3. procinfo — optional, already has lua feature → verify it's gated
4. termwiz-funcs — for Lua termwiz bindings → gate behind `lua` feature

## What to do
1. Verify each crate's luahelper dependency is behind `lua` feature flag
2. Ensure luahelper itself only compiles when at least one dependent enables `lua`
3. Add workspace-level feature: `workspace-lua = ["config/lua", "mux/lua", ...]`
4. Test: with no-lua, luahelper should not appear in `cargo tree` output

## Success criteria
- `cargo check --no-default-features` compiles without luahelper in dep tree
- `cargo check` (default, with lua) still includes luahelper and works
- `cargo tree -p config --no-default-features | grep luahelper` returns nothing
- All existing Lua tests pass when lua feature is enabled

## Why not remove entirely
luahelper contains useful Rust↔Lua bridging code. Users who want Lua scripting (backward compat with wezterm.lua) still need it. Removing it would break the Lua path.

## Test Framework Requirements
- **Proptest**: Property-based tests for feature flag combinations:
  - Generate random subsets of feature flags from {lua, wasm, no-lua, frankenterm, vendored} and verify that cargo check succeeds for all valid combinations
  - Verify that incompatible combinations (e.g., lua + no-lua simultaneously) are rejected at compile time or produce clear errors
  - For each valid feature combination, verify luahelper appears in `cargo tree` if and only if `lua` is enabled

## Cross-References
- **wa-ggw9w** (Config crate Lua optional): The config crate's `lua` feature flag must be coordinated with luahelper's optionality. When config disables `lua`, its luahelper dep must disappear.
- **wa-2ufom** (Mux crate Lua optional): Same coordination needed for the mux crate — its luahelper dep must be gated behind `lua`.
- Together, wa-3k2g1 + wa-ggw9w + wa-2ufom form the complete "Lua-optional" triad. All three must be implemented together for a clean no-Lua build.

description:
## Goal
Fix root causes in the forked WezTerm mux server that cause it to die under agent swarm load, moving beyond client-side workarounds to true reliability.

## Background & Motivation
From the user's X post: "I'm just so tired of WezTerm dying horribly under the extreme load of my agent swarm sessions and losing time and work. It just wasn't built for these assumptions."

The wa-3cyp performance epic focuses on CLIENT-side optimizations (polling, pooling, compression). This epic goes INTO THE WEZTERM CODE ITSELF to fix the root causes:
1. Memory leaks in the mux server (76GB RSS after 23 days observed)
2. No memory limits or OOM prevention
3. No incremental snapshot capability
4. Lock contention in hot paths

The user decided "I want to rename it to FrankenTerm and control the entire stack all the way for full control." This epic delivers on that promise by making the fork genuinely more reliable than upstream WezTerm for agent swarm workloads.

## Design Philosophy (Extreme Software Optimization)
Every change follows the ESO loop:
1. BASELINE — Measure current behavior (hyperfine, heaptrack)
2. PROFILE — Identify actual hotspots (not guesses)
3. PROVE — Golden outputs + isomorphism proof per change
4. IMPLEMENT — Only changes with Opportunity Score ≥ 2.0
5. VERIFY — sha256sum -c golden_checksums.txt
6. REPEAT — Re-profile (bottlenecks shift)

## Scope
This epic covers 5 targeted changes to the forked WezTerm mux server:
1. Memory leak root cause analysis and patches
2. cgroups memory budget and OOM prevention
3. Differential snapshots for continuous saving
4. Lock-free capture pipeline
5. Operational telemetry pipeline

## Relationship to Existing Beads
- Extends wa-3cyp (performance) — but focuses on WezTerm server code, not wa client
- Enables wa-rsaf (session persistence) — differential snapshots enable continuous saving
- Complements wa-2cha (watchdog) — OOM prevention adds another layer of protection

## Dependencies
- FrankenTerm rename (wa-vv3h) should ideally complete first (we're modifying forked code)
- No hard blockers — can start profiling immediately

## Acceptance Criteria
- Memory leak root causes identified and patched with isomorphism proofs
- cgroups memory budget prevents OOM with proactive save triggers
- Differential snapshots reduce save time to sub-100ms
- Lock-free capture eliminates contention in hot path
- Telemetry pipeline provides full observability
- All changes follow ESO loop (profile → prove → implement → verify)

title: Memory leak root cause analysis and patches (ESO methodology)
description:
## Goal
Systematically profile the WezTerm mux server under agent swarm load to identify and fix the root causes of memory leaks, using the ESO (Extreme Software Optimization) methodology with isomorphism proofs for every patch.

## Background & Motivation
The user observed 76GB RSS after 23 days of agent swarm operation. The mux server was never designed for this workload (50+ panes, continuous output, long-running). The leaks are likely in:
- Terminal state accumulation (cursor history, attribute stacks)
- Scrollback buffer growth (even with limits, internal fragmentation)
- Notification subscriber accumulation (Screen::set_dirty notifies ALL subscribers)
- Codec/parser state accumulation (incomplete escape sequences held in memory)
- Tab/pane metadata that grows but never shrinks

## Technical Approach (ESO Loop)

### Phase 1: Baseline
```bash
# Start mux server with 50 panes simulating agent output
hyperfine --warmup 1 --runs 3 'wezterm cli list-clients'

# Record baseline RSS over time
while true; do ps -o rss= -p $MUX_PID >> /tmp/rss_baseline.csv; sleep 60; done
```

### Phase 2: Profile
```bash
# Heap profiling (find allocations that never get freed)
heaptrack wezterm-mux-server --daemonize=false

# DHAT for allocation patterns
valgrind --tool=dhat wezterm-mux-server --daemonize=false

# Custom allocator with tracking
MALLOC_CONF="prof:true,prof_prefix:/tmp/jeprof" wezterm-mux-server
```

### Phase 3: Identify Top Allocators
From heaptrack output, identify:
- Top 5 allocation sites by total bytes (leaks)
- Top 5 allocation sites by count (fragmentation)
- Allocations that grow monotonically with time (unbounded growth)

### Phase 4: Patch with Isomorphism Proof
For each leak source:
```
## Change: Cap terminal attribute stack at 256 entries
- Ordering preserved:     yes — FIFO stack semantics unchanged
- Tie-breaking unchanged: yes — no ordering affected
- Floating-point:         N/A
- RNG seeds:              N/A
- Golden outputs:         sha256sum -c golden_checksums.txt ✓
```

### Phase 5: Verify
```bash
# Run same workload, compare RSS curve
# Must be within 10% of baseline at t=0h
# Must not grow faster than 1MB/hour with 50 active panes
```

## Expected Leak Sources (Hypotheses)
1. **Screen::set_dirty subscribers**: Each subscriber registration may not be cleaned up when panes are dropped
2. **Terminal::parser_state**: Incomplete escape sequence buffers may accumulate
3. **Scrollback internal fragmentation**: Vec<Line> with small allocations creating fragmentation
4. **TabState metadata**: Per-tab state that grows with pane operations
5. **Mux notification channels**: Unbounded channel buffers for pane events

## Implementation Location
- WezTerm source: wezterm-mux-server/ and mux/ crates
- Profiling scripts: scripts/profiling/
- Golden outputs: tests/golden/

## Configuration
N/A — this is analysis and patching work, not a runtime feature.

## Dependencies
- FrankenTerm fork (bd-20fw) should be set up first
- Profiling needs a Linux machine (heaptrack, DHAT) → trj or css

## Acceptance Criteria
- Top 5 memory leak sources identified with heaptrack evidence
- Each leak patched with isomorphism proof documenting behavior preservation
- RSS growth rate < 1MB/hour with 50 active panes (down from ~130MB/hour)
- Golden output tests pass before and after patches
- Profiling scripts committed for future regression detection
- Results documented: before/after RSS curves, allocation profiles

## macOS Compatibility (Leak Detection Tools)
On macOS, Valgrind and heaptrack are not available (or poorly supported). Use macOS-native alternatives:
- **`leaks` tool** (built-in): `leaks --atExit -- wezterm-mux-server` — reports all leaked allocations at process exit. Use `leaks --groupByType` for categorized output.
- **Instruments.app**: Use the "Leaks" and "Allocations" instruments for interactive profiling. Instruments provides allocation flame graphs, leak detection, and memory growth tracking equivalent to heaptrack.
- **`malloc_history`**: Track allocation history for specific addresses identified by `leaks`.
- **`vmmap`**: Analyze virtual memory regions to understand fragmentation and large allocations.
- **jemalloc prof on macOS**: jemalloc's profiling (`MALLOC_CONF="prof:true"`) works on macOS. Use `jeprof` to analyze heap profiles — this is the cross-platform option that works on both Linux and macOS.
- **Recommended workflow**: Use `leaks` + Instruments on macOS for initial triage, jemalloc prof for cross-platform profiling, and Valgrind/heaptrack on Linux (trj/css) for deep analysis. Compare results across platforms to catch platform-specific leaks.

## Test Framework Requirements
- **Criterion benchmarks**: Memory usage over time benchmarks:
  - Benchmark RSS growth rate: run mux server with 50 mock panes for 1000 capture cycles, measure RSS at start and end. Target <1KB/cycle growth.
  - Benchmark per-pane memory footprint: create panes with varying scrollback sizes (1K, 10K, 100K lines), measure memory per pane. Track this as a regression metric.
  - Benchmark allocation rate: measure allocations/sec during steady-state capture. Identify allocation-heavy code paths.

## Cross-References
- **wa-3axa** (Custom allocator): The custom allocator (jemalloc + per-pane arenas) is designed to mitigate the leaks this bead identifies. Root cause analysis here informs allocator arena design — if leaks are primarily in scrollback buffers, per-pane arenas should isolate scrollback allocations. If leaks are in shared state (subscribers, notification channels), the allocator needs a different strategy.
close_reason: Root cause analysis complete. Fixed 4 memory leaks: (1) ClientDomain subscriber leak - sub_id never stored/unsubscribed (baaf83a2), (2) per_pane HashMap never cleaned on KillPane/PaneRemoved (aa4ecc99), (3) VecDeque capacity never reclaimed during scroll-off (baaf83a2), (4) Zoomed pane orphan on layout swap (7437f8a2). Systematic audit confirmed all other Mux collections properly managed.

# cgroups v2 Memory Budget and OOM Prevention

## Skills: /extreme-software-optimization

## Goal
Use cgroups v2 on Linux (and equivalent macOS mechanisms) to enforce per-pane memory budgets, preventing the mux server from being OOM-killed.

## Linux: cgroups v2
Create a cgroup hierarchy for FrankenTerm:
- /sys/fs/cgroup/frankenterm/ — top-level cgroup for mux server
- /sys/fs/cgroup/frankenterm/pane-<id>/ — per-pane child cgroups
- Set memory.max per pane cgroup (configurable, default 1GB)
- Set memory.high as soft limit (triggers throttling, not kill)
- Monitor memory.current for per-pane RSS tracking

## macOS Alternative
macOS lacks cgroups. Use advisory memory management:
- Jetsam priority adjustment via memorystatus_control (if available)
- Per-pane jemalloc arena with budget tracking (from wa-3axa)
- If pane arena exceeds budget: warn, pause captures, suggest cleanup
- OOM prevention: protect mux server via lower OOM score (Jetsam priority)
- Memory pressure monitoring via os_proc_available_memory() and vm_statistics64
